content: Oral hygiene refers to the practice of maintaining cleanliness in the mouth and on the teeth to prevent dental issues such as cavities, gum disease, and bad breath. Teeth cleaning involves the removal of dental plaque and tartar from the teeth to prevent conditions like cavities, gingivitis, and periodontal disease. Gum disease, in particular, is a leading cause of tooth loss in adults. Dentists recommend professional teeth cleaning at least twice a year. This process typically includes tooth scaling, polishing, and, in cases of significant tartar accumulation, debridement. Following professional cleaning, a fluoride treatment is often applied to strengthen the teeth. However, maintaining good oral hygiene between professional cleanings is critical to prevent tartar buildup. This includes regular and thorough brushing with a toothbrush and the use of dental floss to remove plaque-forming bacteria from the teeth. Gum care is also an essential component of oral hygiene. Massaging the gums is often recommended to promote healthy gum tissue and improve overall oral health. Diet and oral hygiene are closely linked. Foods that support muscle and bone health also benefit the teeth and gums. Dairy products, for example, provide vitamin D, which strengthens teeth. Breads and cereals are rich in vitamin B, while fruits and vegetables supply vitamin C, both of which are essential for healthy gum tissue. Lean meats, fish, and poultry contribute magnesium and zinc, which are important for dental health. Brushing the teeth after every meal and before bedtime is often advised, along with flossing at least once daily, preferably at night. For some individuals, flossing after every meal may be recommended. Foods high in fiber and sugar-free chewing gum can also stimulate saliva production, which helps neutralize acids and clean the teeth. Sugars are strongly associated with the development of dental cavities. While sucrose (table sugar) is the most common culprit, other sugars like glucose and maltose are equally harmful. Cooked starches, such as potato chips, can also contribute to tooth decay, though to a lesser extent, as they must first be broken down by enzymes in saliva. To minimize the risk of cavities, it is important to limit sugary foods and drinks to mealtimes, allowing the teeth time to repair themselves. Natural sugars found in fruits and fruit juices can also contribute to cavities, as these foods often contain acids that lower the pH in the mouth. For example, citrus fruits like oranges, lemons, and limes are acidic. In contrast, carbonic acid in sugar-free soda water is only weakly acidic and does not contribute to cavities. However, sugary soft drinks significantly increase the risk of cavities, especially when consumed throughout the day. Sticky foods, particularly those high in sugar, can adhere to the teeth and prolong the time the mouth remains at a low pH, increasing the risk of decay. To maintain oral health, it is essential to brush the teeth at least twice daily with fluoride toothpaste and to use dental floss to remove food particles and plaque. Chewing sugar-free gum can also help clean the teeth and stimulate saliva production, though it may dislodge loose fillings in individuals with poor dental health. Smoking and chewing tobacco are associated with numerous dental problems, including gum disease and oral cancer. Dental gums are marketed as beneficial for oral health. Appliances such as retainers, braces, and dentures require meticulous cleaning to maintain hygiene.
